summary: Research, verify and chain 40 quotes on: the value of time, do what matters now, stay strong and healthy to have more time

lines.line: Watch a river. It never stops, day or night. Neither does your time.
And while we keep saying 'later', life speeds right past us.
Too late to start? Midlife starters did nearly as well as lifelong movers.
So move tomorrow's job to today, and today's job to right now.
Then shoot like you have one arrow. No second try. This one counts.
A cellist of 81 practised hours daily. Why? He felt he was still improving.
And yoga asks for balance: food, sleep, work, never too much or too little.
Can you get down to the floor and up easily? That predicted longer life.
Not just longer. Real life is living in good health.
So, to all who practise: don't let your time flow past unused. Practise today.
Our life is a dewdrop on the grass. The sun is already rising.
No day gets a second morning. Use this one: the years won't wait.
Looking back, no one regretted learning a skill. They regretted what they never did.
Hard to get up? Remember: you rise to do a human being's work.
Then treat this morning's practice as a meeting that comes once in a lifetime.
Mornings start the night before. Basketball players who slept more ran faster, shot better.
Add the basics: moderate exercise, and just enough food to refuel, not overload.
At 107 she released her sixth piano album. She said youth lives inside us.
While your body is well, put your biggest effort into what matters most.
For 80 years, a master began each morning playing music he loved. Begin yours.
One Olympic marathon took him 54 years. A happy life happened along the way.
After 30, muscle slowly fades. Training and good food can change that a lot.
A nun began training at 48. At 82, she crossed an Ironman finish line.
No time? Five to ten minutes of slow running daily went with longer life.
Small or big, whatever task you find, give it all your strength.
That is what yoga means: doing each action with skill and care.
At 105 he sprinted 100 metres in Kyoto. His secret: health comes first.
And health starts at the table: stop eating at about 80% full.
Lifelong skiers in their 80s had the fitness of untrained men 40 years younger.
One day lived with full effort beats a hundred lazy years. Make it today.
Every minute is gold. You're spending some right now, reading this.
Yet we keep promising 'tomorrow.' Thai even has a saying for that.
Yesterday is gone. Tomorrow hasn't come. Today is the day to work hard.
Still dancing at 100, she heard 'I wish I could.' Her answer: do it.
But our minds wander almost half the time, and that costs us happiness.
The fix: give each thing your whole mind. On the mat, only the mat.
Richer than gold: health. It's the root of goodness, wealth, joy and inner freedom.
Even under 75 minutes of brisk walking a week went with 1.8 extra years.
Long life pays interest: each day you learn, each month you can do more.
Now is the only time you can use. So spend it on the mat.

final.checks:
BASE: Draft B's four carousels (River, Morning, Finish Line, Gold). Each slide sets up a question or a gap that the next slide answers, and each central image comes back on slide 10. Lines from Draft A were grafted in where they were stronger.

GRAFTS FROM DRAFT A
- C1 hook: "Watch a river... Neither does your time." The point comes in the last words, so it stops the scroll better than B's version.
- Y1 hook: "Our life is a dewdrop on the grass. The sun is already rising." It reads as a hard truth and also as a hopeful morning. It leads straight into C4, "No day gets a second morning."
- B2: written in the past tense ("Looking back, no one regretted..."). This matches the study and does not overstate it.
- S3: "Still dancing at 100, she heard 'I wish I could.' Her answer: do it." The story is clearer than in B.
- S1: B's line plus A's "Olympic" for higher stakes.

ID SWAP
- Y3 (Buddha: past is behind, future not here, today is the day to work) replaces W2 (Seneca) in Gold.
- Y3 is the most direct statement of Boonchu's theme ("now, not some long-term plan"), and B had left it out.
- Gold now runs: gold minute, Thai "tomorrow" habit, today is the day, "do it".
- There is no other Buddha line in Gold.

FAITHFULNESS FIXES
- C14 (Shitou): B made him say "the river won't stop", which is not in his quote. Now: "don't let your time flow past unused. Practise today." The river is only hinted at through the verb.
- Y8 (Gita): "Yoga that lasts" added a claim the Gita does not make. Now: "And yoga asks for balance..."
- W12 (Martial): reframed as "Not just longer. Real life is living in good health." It now follows on from B8 and keeps Martial's meaning.
- B10: "1.8 extra years" was stated as a cause, and "75 minutes" was a range. Now: "Even under 75 minutes... went with 1.8 extra years."
- B4: removed the awkward "slow running minutes".
- C13 (Tolstoy): "the only time you can use", which is closer to "the only time we have any power". It keeps the gold image with "spend it on the mat".
- W10: "gentle" changed back to the source's "moderate".
- Y7: "by the way" removed. It is hard for language learners.
- W8 (Montaigne): "be all there" changed to "give each thing your whole mind". The idiom was unclear for learners.
- C5: the old "a saying for it" had nothing for "it" to refer to. It now links to the gold minute with "Yet we keep promising 'tomorrow.'" This echoes the Thai idiom without showing the literal original.

RULES, CHECKED BY SCRIPT
- 4 carousels of 10 lines, 40 unique ids.
- Every line is 14 words or fewer. The longest is 14.
- No long dashes, no "pose", and no flood, storm or tide images.

STAGES AND SPREAD
- Every carousel runs in arc order: time_passes, dont_wait, do_your_best, strong_body, more_time, payoff.
- No author appears twice in one carousel. Casals, Seneca, Krishna, the Buddha, Confucius-era Chinese sources and Martial are each split across carousels.
- Every carousel has a yoga or Indian text, an Asian source, a Western source, a sport or old-master story, and science.
- Thai (C5) and Russian (Tolstoy C13) are both in Gold. Chinese sources are in every carousel.

TONE AND FACTS
- Science lines say "went with" or "predicted", never that something causes something.
- Age and death come through warm stories: the 107-year-old pianist, the 105-year-old sprinter, the nun at 82.
- Every slide 10 points to practice today: "Practise today", "Begin yours", "Make it today", "spend it on the mat".

UNUSED BUT STRONG BACKUPS: W13 (Martial, "too late is tomorrow's life"), B13 (no upper limit on fitness benefit), W14 (Emerson), S13 (Grandma Moses), C10 (Russian proverb).

verified.quote: It's like a drop of dew on a grass tip. When the sun comes up it vanishes right away and doesn't last long. In the same way, life as a human is like a dewdrop.
verified.original: Seyyathāpi, brāhmaṇa, tiṇagge ussāvabindu sūriye uggacchante khippaṁyeva paṭivigacchati, na ciraṭṭhitikaṁ hoti; evamevaṁ kho, brāhmaṇa, ussāvabindūpamaṁ jīvitaṁ manussānaṁ ... (Pali)
verified.who: The Buddha, retelling the teaching of an ancient teacher named Araka
verified.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.74 (Araka Sutta), segments 2.1-2.2, tr. Bhikkhu Sujato, SuttaCentral, 2018 (CC0)
verified.meaning: Human life is short, like dew on grass that vanishes when the sun rises.
verified.reason: I opened the Sujato translation and the Pali root file. The wording matches segment 2.1 and the first sentence of 2.2 word for word, and Araka is the speaker inside the Buddha's account. SuttaCentral's publication data gives AN as first published 2018 under CC0. The 36,000 figure in 10.10 is 'chattiṁsaṁyeva rattisahassāni' (36,000 nights), so the note is correct. The dew image is gentle and has no rising water. Leave out the other similes (bubbles in heavy rain, a line in water, a fast river, a cow led to slaughter). Not in the used list.

verified.quote: Time flies, nights pass by, the stages of life leave us one by one.
verified.original: Accenti kālā tarayanti rattiyo, vayoguṇā anupubbaṁ jahanti (Pali)
verified.who: A deity speaks the verse to the Buddha, and the Buddha's reply repeats these same two lines
verified.source: Samyutta Nikaya 1.4 (Accenti Sutta, 'Time Flies'), verses 2.1-2.2 and 3.1-3.2, tr. Bhikkhu Sujato, SuttaCentral, 2018 (CC0)
verified.meaning: Time keeps moving, and the stages of life pass by one by one.
verified.reason: Checked against the Sujato JSON and the Pali root. The two lines are exact and appear in both verses: the deity's (2.1-2.2) and the reply (3.1-3.2). Crediting the Samyutta Nikaya rather than 'the Buddha said' is the honest choice. Stopping before 'Seeing this peril in death' keeps it gentle. SN was first published in 2018 under CC0. Not in the used list (SN 6.1, 22.101 and 45.49 were used).

verified.quote: Don't run back to the past, don't anticipate the future. What's past is left behind, the future has not arrived... Today's the day to keenly work.
verified.original: Atītaṁ nānvāgameyya, nappaṭikaṅkhe anāgataṁ; yadatītaṁ pahīnaṁ taṁ, appattañca anāgataṁ ... Ajjeva kiccamātappaṁ (Pali)
verified.who: The Buddha
verified.source: Majjhima Nikaya 131 (Bhaddekaratta Sutta, 'One Fine Night'), verse at 3.1-3.4 and 3.9, tr. Bhikkhu Sujato, SuttaCentral, 2018 (CC0)
verified.meaning: Don't live in the past or the future. Today is the day to work.
verified.credit: The Buddha · Majjhima Nikaya 131, tr. Sujato
verified.reason: Lines 3.1-3.4 and 3.9 match the Sujato text exactly. The ellipsis leaves out 3.5-3.8, which does not change the sense. The Buddha speaks the verse himself as the 'summary recital'. The source line now names the exact segments used. End at 'keenly work': the next line is 'who knows, tomorrow may bring death!', which is too dark. MN was first published 2018 under CC0. Not in the used list (MN 26, 36 and 107 were used).

verified.quote: Get up and meditate! What's the point in your sleeping? ... Don't let the moment pass you by.
verified.original: Uṭṭhahatha nisīdatha, ko attho supitena vo ... khaṇo vo mā upaccagā (Pali)
verified.who: Sutta Nipata verse, traditionally counted as the Buddha's words
verified.source: Sutta Nipata 2.10 (Utthana Sutta, 'Get Up!'), verses 1.1-1.2 and 3.4, tr. Bhikkhu Sujato, 'Anthology of Discourses', SuttaCentral, first published 2021 (CC0)
verified.meaning: Get up and practise. Don't let this moment slip away.
verified.reason: The text is exact (1.1-1.2 and 3.4), and the Pali matches. One fix: the date. SuttaCentral's publication record (scpub17) gives Sujato's Sutta Nipata as first published in 2021, not 2018. The '...' correctly leaves out the arrow wound, the 'King of Death' and 'you'll grieve when sent to hell'. Crediting the collection, not a direct 'Buddha said', is right because the poem names no speaker. Not in the used list.

verified.quote: What you would do tomorrow, do today; what you would do today, do now.
verified.original: काल करै सो आज कर आज करैं सो अब्ब। (kāl karai so āj kar, āj karaiṁ so abb) (Old Hindi; first line of the couplet as printed in Kavita-Kaumudi, 1918)
verified.who: Hindi saying, traditionally attributed to Kabir (authorship not established)
verified.source: Printed as a Kabir saakhi, no. 19, in Kavita-Kaumudi vol. 1, ed. Ramnaresh Tripathi, 1918 (Hindi Wikisource transcription). Literal English translation.
verified.meaning: Do tomorrow's job today, and today's job right now.
verified.reason: I opened the Wikisource page: it is saakhi no. 19 under Kabir, and the page header dates Kavita-Kaumudi to 1918. Fix: the printing reads 'आज करैं' (with anusvara), so the original now matches it. I found no scholarly source tying it to Kabir himself, and Kabir's verses were passed on orally with many later additions. It is therefore usable only with the label 'Hindi saying, attributed to Kabir', never 'Kabir said'. Use only the first line. The second line's 'parlai' (pralay, cosmic dissolution, often pictured as a deluge) breaks the no-flood rule. The used list has three other Kabir passages, but not this one.

verified.quote: If anything is to be done, let a man do it, let him attack it vigorously!
verified.original: Kayirā ce kayirāthenaṁ, daḷhamenaṁ parakkame (Pali)
verified.who: The Buddha
verified.source: Dhammapada 313 (ch. XXII, 'The Downward Course'), tr. F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 10, 1881
verified.meaning: If something is worth doing, do it with all your strength.
verified.credit: The Buddha · Dhammapada 313, tr. Max Müller
verified.reason: The Gutenberg text has verse 313 word for word, in Chapter XXII 'The Downward Course' (SBE vol. X). It is public domain. Leave out the second half ('A careless pilgrim only scatters the dust of his passions'). The chapter is about the hell realms, but this verse is not, so no hell content appears on the slide. Not in the used list (Dhp 19, 80, 81, 204 and 239 were used). The backup Dhp 276 is also in this file at line 1145.

verified.quote: ...therefore cleave thou to yoga; yoga is skill in action.
verified.original: तस्माद्योगाय युज्यस्व योगः कर्मसु कौशलम् (tasmād yogāya yujyasva yogaḥ karmasu kauśalam) (Sanskrit)
verified.who: Krishna, in the Bhagavad Gita
verified.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.50, tr. Annie Besant, The Bhagavad-Gita, 4th ed., 1922 (Wikisource transcription)
verified.meaning: Yoga means doing your work with real skill and care.
verified.reason: The Wikisource page has verse (50) exactly: 'United to the Pure Reason one abandoneth here both good and evil deeds; therefore cleave thou to yoga; yoga is skill in action.' The page header dates this edition to 1922. The Sanskrit half-line matches. Besant died in 1933, so the text is public domain. 'Skill in action' (karmasu kauśalam) is faithfully reflected in the meaning line. 2.50 is not among the used Gita verses.

verified.quote: Verily yoga is not for him who eateth too much, nor who abstaineth to excess, nor who is too much addicted to sleep, nor even to wakefulness, O Arjuna. Yoga killeth out all pain for him who is regulated in eating and amusement, regulated in performing actions, regulated in sleeping and waking.
verified.original: नात्यश्नतस्तु योगोऽस्ति न चैकान्तमनश्नतः । न चातिस्वप्नशीलस्य जाग्रतो नैव चार्जुन ॥ युक्ताहारविहारस्य युक्तचेष्टस्य कर्मसु । युक्तस्वप्नावबोधस्य योगो भवति दुःखहा ॥ (Sanskrit)
verified.who: Krishna, in the Bhagavad Gita
verified.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.16-17, tr. Annie Besant, The Bhagavad-Gita, 4th ed., 1922 (Wikisource transcription)
verified.meaning: Yoga needs balance: not too much or too little food, sleep, or work.
verified.reason: Verses (16) and (17) on the Discourse 6 page match exactly, and so does the Sanskrit. It is public domain. The used list has Gita 6.19, 6.23-25, 6.35 and 6.40, but not 6.16-17. The text is two sentences long, so for a short slide use 6.17 alone. It fits the theme's 'moderation, rest' with no unsafe content.

verified.quote: Health is the supreme foundation of virtue, wealth, enjoyment and salvation.
verified.original: धर्मार्थकाममोक्षाणामारोग्यं मूलमुत्तमम् (dharmārthakāmamokṣāṇām ārogyaṁ mūlam uttamam) (Sanskrit)
verified.who: The great sages gathered to seek the science of long life, in the Charaka Samhita
verified.source: Charaka Samhita, Sutrasthana 1.15 (ch. 1, 'The Quest for Longevity'), tr. Shree Gulabkunverba Ayurvedic Society, Jamnagar, 1949 (wisdomlib transcription); Sanskrit at carakasamhitaonline.com, Deerghanjiviteeya Adhyaya
verified.meaning: Good health is the root of goodness, success, joy and inner freedom.
verified.reason: The wisdomlib text (verses 15-16½) begins with this exact sentence, spoken by the assembled sages. On carakasamhitaonline the Sanskrit is numbered ||15||. Stop here: the next sentence is 'diseases are the destroyers of health... and even of life itself', which is an illness scare. Copyright note: the 1949 Jamnagar translation may still be protected in some countries. A one-line quote is low risk, and the same translation was used before (Su 7.32). For full safety, use a fresh literal rendering: 'Health is the supreme root of dharma, artha, kama and moksha.'

verified.quote: When a man is always mindful, knowing moderation in eating, his discomfort fades, and he ages slowly, taking care of his life.
verified.original: Manujassa sadā satīmato, mattaṁ jānato laddhabhojane; tanukassa bhavanti vedanā, saṇikaṁ jīrati āyupālayan (Pali)
verified.who: The Buddha
verified.source: Samyutta Nikaya 3.13 (Donapaka Sutta, 'A Bucketful of Rice'), verse 3.1-3.4, tr. Bhikkhu Sujato, SuttaCentral, 2018 (CC0)
verified.meaning: Eat mindfully and not too much, and you will age slowly.
verified.credit: The Buddha · Samyutta Nikaya 3.13, tr. Sujato
verified.reason: The verse matches 3.1-3.4 exactly, and the Pali is confirmed. ROYALTY FLAG confirmed: the setting is King Pasenadi eating rice by the bucketful. The verse itself names no king. Use it with the credit only, and do not tell the story or show any king imagery. 'Saṇikaṁ jīrati āyupālayaṁ' (ages slowly, guarding life) links health to more years. SN was first published 2018 under CC0. Not in the used list.

verified.quote: The disciplined man that practises wholesome diet lives for a period of 36000 nights i.e. hundred years blessed by good men and free from disease.
verified.original: षट्त्रिंशतं सहस्राणि रात्रीणां हितभोजनः। जीवत्यनातुरो जन्तुर्जितात्मा सम्मतः सताम्॥ (ṣaṭtriṁśataṁ sahasrāṇi rātrīṇāṁ hitabhojanaḥ, jīvaty anāturo jantur jitātmā sammataḥ satām) (Sanskrit)
verified.who: Charaka Samhita (teaching of Atreya, as compiled by Agnivesha and revised by Charaka)
verified.source: Charaka Samhita, Sutrasthana 27.348 (ch. 27, 'Diet and Dietetics'), tr. Shree Gulabkunverba Ayurvedic Society, Jamnagar, 1949 (wisdomlib transcription); Sanskrit at carakasamhitaonline.com, Annapanavidhi Adhyaya
verified.meaning: Eat wisely and live with self-control, and you can live a hundred healthy years.
verified.reason: Verse 348 on wisdomlib matches word for word. Carakasamhitaonline gives the same verse at ||348|| (it spells the first word ṣaḍtriṁśataṁ) with an almost identical English. Present it as an ancient Ayurvedic ideal ('the old texts say'), not as medical data or a promise. It pairs with Y1's 36,000 nights. Copyright caveat as for Y9; a fresh literal rendering is easy. Not in the used list (only Su 7.32 was used).

verified.quote: If (one's food has been) digested let one eat with moderation; (for) that is the way to prolong the life of an embodied soul.
verified.original: அற்றால் அளவறிந்து உண்க அஃதுடம்பு பெற்றான் நெடிதுய்க்கும் ஆறு. (aṟṟāl aḷavaṟintu uṇka aḥtuṭampu peṟṟāṉ neṭituykkum āṟu) (Tamil, Parimelalakar's reading; Project Madurai and thirukkural.net read அறவறிந்து)
verified.who: Tiruvalluvar
verified.source: Tirukkural 943 (ch. 95, 'Medicine'), English prose rendering from the Drew and Lazarus translation (completed by John Lazarus, 1885), as printed in the Project Madurai e-text 'Tirukkural, English Translation and Commentary by Pope, Drew, Lazarus and Ellis' (from a reprint of Pope's 1886 W. H. Allen edition). Tamil per Parimelalakar's commentary text on Tamil Wikisource.
verified.meaning: Eat in moderation, after your last meal is digested, to live long.
verified.reason: The English prose and Pope's couplet for 943 under '2.3.22. Medicine' match exactly. Fix 1, the Tamil: thirukkural.net and Project Madurai's Tamil e-text both read 'அறவறிந்து', not the 'அளவறிந்து' given. 'அளவறிந்து' is Parimelalakar's reading (ta.wikisource.org, Tirukkural Parimelazhagar Urai, Porutpal 95. Marundhu), and that is the reading the English 'with moderation' follows. Fix 2, the translator: Project Madurai says the 1886 edition was reprinted in 1962 and 1982. Claiming the prose appeared in the 1886 'Sacred Kural' itself is not supported, so credit the e-text. Public domain. Used kurals were 415, 475 and 620, so 943 is new.

verified.quote: As long [as] this body is free from disease... so long wise persons should put forth mighty exertions for the sake of their supreme good.
verified.original: यावत्स्वस्थमिदं शरीरमरुजं यावज्जरा दूरतो यावच्चेन्द्रियशक्तिरप्रतिहता यावत्क्षयो नायुषः । आत्मश्रेयसि तावदेव विदुषा कार्यः प्रयत्नो महान् ... (Sanskrit)
verified.who: Bhartrihari (traditional author of the Vairagya Shataka)
verified.source: Bhartrihari, Vairagya Shataka, verse 75, tr. 'The Editors' (Prabuddha Bharata / Advaita Ashrama; later editions credit Swami Madhavananda), The Vairagya-Satakam or The Hundred Verses on Renunciation, Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916
verified.meaning: While your body is healthy and strong, make your big effort now.
verified.reason: The 1916 scan has verse 75 exactly as the item gives it, with the OCR misspelling 'desease'. Sanskrit verse ७५ is confirmed at sanskritdocuments.org/doc_z_misc_major_works/vairagya.html. The 1916 Indian printing is public domain. The fix is for content safety only: the full line stacks 'disease and decrepitude', 'senility' and 'life... decaying', plus the burning-house image, and together these read as morbid for a hopeful carousel. This shorter, still faithful excerpt keeps the theme (act while healthy). '[as]' fills a word the 1916 printer dropped. The Vivekananda rendering was not checked, so do not use it. Bhartrihari is not in the used list.

verified.quote: And he who lives a hundred years, idle and weak, a life of one day is better if a man has attained firm strength.
verified.original: Yo ca vassasataṁ jīve, kusīto hīnavīriyo; ekāhaṁ jīvitaṁ seyyo, vīriyamārabhato daḷhaṁ (Pali)
verified.who: The Buddha
verified.source: Dhammapada 112 (ch. VIII, 'The Thousands'), tr. F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 10, 1881
verified.meaning: One day lived with real effort beats a hundred lazy years.
verified.credit: The Buddha · Dhammapada 112, tr. Max Müller
verified.reason: Verse 112 in Chapter VIII 'The Thousands' of the Gutenberg Müller text matches word for word. It is public domain. The Pali 'vīriyam ārabhato daḷhaṁ' means 'of one who rouses firm energy', so the meaning line ('real effort') is faithful and does not refer to muscles. Not in the used list. It can also serve do_your_best.

verified.quote: The Master standing by a stream, said, 'It passes on just like this, not ceasing day or night!'
verified.original: 子在川上曰：逝者如斯夫！不舍晝夜。
verified.who: Confucius
verified.source: Analects IX.17 (Legge numbers it IX.16), tr. James Legge, The Chinese Classics vol. 1 (first published 1861), Project Gutenberg #4094
verified.meaning: Time keeps flowing past, day and night, and never stops.
verified.reason: I downloaded Gutenberg #4094 and checked it. The English matches word for word (CHAP. XVI), and the Chinese printed beside it is 子在川上曰、逝者如斯夫、不舍晝夜. The used list only has Analects IX.10 (Yan Hui) and IX.18 (basketful) from this book, so this passage is new. On safety, it is a calm stream: no flood, storm, tide or rising water. But with the Thai floods, do not show any water in the visuals. Use a sundial, a dawn sky or a mat. If you want no water at all, lead with C2 instead.

verified.quote: Reading, I did not notice spring had grown deep. An inch of time is an inch of gold.
verified.original: 讀書不覺已春深，一寸光陰一寸金。
verified.who: Wang Zhenbai, Tang dynasty poet (passed the jinshi exam in 895)
verified.source: Two Poems at White Deer Grotto (白鹿洞二首), poem 1, lines 1-2; literal translation
verified.meaning: Every little bit of time is as precious as gold.
verified.reason: Wikisource gives poem 1 under 王貞白 (Tang) with these exact lines. Chinese Wikipedia (王贞白) confirms he passed the jinshi in 乾宁二年, 895, and that this line is his famous one. The literal translation is faithful. The follow-on line 寸金難買寸光陰 is NOT his. Search results trace it to the Ming novel 三寶太監西洋記, but I did not open that text, so if it is used at all, label it only 'Chinese saying'. I also confirmed the Huainanzi 原道訓 line (時不與人游…重寸之陰，時難得而易失也) on Wikisource. The sentence right after it is about the ruler Yu, so leave it out. Not in the used list.

verified.quote: No man is careful of small moments of time... Therefore the Wise Man will not be careful of far-off days and months, but rather careful lest the Present Moment pass unprofitably.
verified.original: 寸陰惜しむ人なし。……されば、道人は、遠く日月を惜しむべからず。ただ今の一念、空しく過ぐる事を惜しむべし。
verified.who: Yoshida Kenko, Japanese monk and essayist
verified.source: Tsurezuregusa (Essays in Idleness) 108, c. 1330; tr. G. B. Sansom, The Tsuredzure Gusa of Yoshida no Kaneyoshi, 1911
verified.meaning: Don't fret over months far away; just don't waste this moment.
verified.reason: I downloaded the archive.org text of Sansom's 1911 translation, and section 108 matches word for word. The Japanese on tsurezuregusa.com/108dan matches too (寸陰惜しむ人なし…されば、道人は、遠く日月を惜しむべからず。たゞ今の一念、空しく過ぐる事を惜しむべし). The '...' correctly leaves out 'of a sudden we reach the term of life' and the 'die tomorrow' part. Kenko 52 and 150 are used, but 108 is new. One caution: Sansom died in 1965. The 1911 printing is public domain in the US but may not be in life+70 countries. 'Prefer PD' is a preference, and Kenko 52 in Sansom's translation was already used, so it is acceptable.

verified.quote: The prime of life does not come twice; a day can hardly have a second morning. Seize the moment and spur yourself on: the years wait for no one.
verified.original: 盛年不重來，一日難再晨。及時當勉勵，歲月不待人。
verified.who: Tao Yuanming (365-427), poet
verified.source: Miscellaneous Poems (雜詩十二首), no. 1, in the Collected Works of Tao Yuanming (陶淵明集), juan 4; literal translation
verified.meaning: Your best years and today's morning come only once. Time won't wait.
verified.reason: I fetched the Wikisource page for 陶淵明集/卷四 and checked it. 雜詩 其一 ends exactly 盛年不重來，一日難再晨。及時當勉勵，歲月不待人. The line before is 得歡當作樂，斗酒聚比鄰 (wine with the neighbours), so in the poem 'spur yourself on' means 'live fully now', not 'study hard'. The meaning line keeps to 'live now', and nothing in the quote mentions alcohol, so it is acceptable. Do not frame it as 'work harder' and do not picture drinking. The translation is the item's own literal one, and it is faithful. Not used before.

verified.quote: Thai idiom: phat wan prakan phrung, 'put off the day, promise tomorrow': to keep postponing, again and again.
verified.original: ผัดวันประกันพรุ่ง
verified.who: Thai idiom (สำนวน)
verified.source: ORST Thai Dictionary (online), sub-entry of ผัด, marked (สำ) ก. and defined ขอเลื่อนเวลาออกไปครั้งแล้วครั้งเล่า; same definition in Thai Wiktionary; Thai PBS 'ตื่นมาเต้น : สำนวน ผัดวันประกันพรุ่ง', 23 Dec 2021
verified.url: https://th.wiktionary.org/wiki/ผัดวันประกันพรุ่ง
verified.meaning: Thai has a saying for 'I'll start tomorrow' again and again. Start today.
verified.credit: Thai idiom · phat wan prakan phrung
verified.reason: I reached the ORST dictionary lookup service (dictionary.orst.go.th/func_lookup.php). It returns ผัดวันประกันพรุ่ง (สำ) ก. ขอเลื่อนเวลาออกไปครั้งแล้วครั้งเล่า, under ผัด. That is the authoritative source, now added. The Wiktionary entry gives the same definition and the RTGS spelling phat-wan-pra-kan-phrung. The Thai PBS segment (aired 23 ธ.ค. 64) defines it as putting things off without ever starting, and it pairs the idiom with morning exercise. The word-by-word gloss is reasonable. Safe, and not in the used list.

verified.quote: Beginners ought not to hold two arrows. They rely on their second arrow and are careless about the first. You ought each time to think, without any idea of missing and hitting, 'This is the shot which counts.'
verified.original: 初心の人、二つの矢を持つ事なかれ。後の矢を頼みて、始めの矢に等閑の心あり。毎度、たゞ、得失なく、この一矢に定むべしと思へ。
verified.who: An archery teacher, as recorded by Yoshida Kenko
verified.source: Tsurezuregusa 92, c. 1330; tr. G. B. Sansom, 1911
verified.meaning: Don't count on a second try. Give this one shot everything.
verified.reason: The Sansom text (archive.org djvu.txt), section 92, matches word for word except for the OCR's stray apostrophe ('without' any'), which is correctly removed. The Japanese on tsurezuregusa.com/092dan matches (初心の人、二つの矢を持つ事なかれ…毎度、たゞ、得失なく、この一矢に定むべしと思へ). The same chapter's 'To-morrow…To-night… Why is it so hard to do a thing Now' line is also confirmed. The OCR reads 'when one, thinks', so drop that comma if you use it. Archery here is a practice, not war. Not used before. If you use C3 as well, that puts two Kenko slides in one carousel.

verified.quote: From the moment you enter the garden path until you leave, honour the host as if this gathering came only once in your lifetime.
verified.original: 路地ヘ入ルヨリ出ヅルマデ、一期ニ一度ノ会ノヤウニ、亭主ヲ敬ヒ畏ベシ (the origin of 一期一会, ichigo ichie)
verified.who: Yamanoue Soji, tea master and student of Sen no Rikyu
verified.source: Yamanoue Soji ki (山上宗二記), section 茶湯者覚悟十体; dated copies 1588-1590; quoted in Nihon Daihyakka Zensho (Nipponica) and Nihon Kokugo Daijiten on Kotobank; literal translation
verified.meaning: Treat each meeting as if it happens only once in your life.
verified.reason: Kotobank's Nipponica entry quotes exactly 路地ヘ入ルヨリ出ヅルマデ、一期ニ一度ノ会ノヤウニ、亭主ヲ敬ヒ畏ベシ as the first appearance of the idea. Nihon Kokugo Daijiten and Kotowaza dictionaries confirm the source is 宗二, Rikyu's student, in 山上宗二記‐茶湯者覚悟十体. They also confirm that the four-character phrase comes later, from 茶湯一会集, c. 1845. Nipponica's 山上宗二記 entry shows the copies are dated from 天正16 (1588) to 天正18 (1590), so the source line now says that. Leave out Ii Naosuke (a statesman) and how Soji died. The translation is faithful. This is a different text from the used Rikyu poems and the Book of Tea passage.

verified.quote: He is simply a man, who in his eager pursuit (of knowledge) forgets his food, who in the joy of its attainment forgets his sorrows, and who does not perceive that old age is coming on.
verified.original: 其為人也，發憤忘食，樂以忘憂，不知老之將至云爾。
verified.who: Confucius, describing himself
verified.source: Analects VII.19 (Legge numbers it VII.18), tr. James Legge, The Chinese Classics vol. 1 (first published 1861), Project Gutenberg #4094
verified.meaning: So eager he forgot to eat; so joyful he didn't notice getting old.
verified.reason: I checked Gutenberg #4094. CHAP. XVIII.2 matches word for word, and the Chinese beside it is 其為人也、發憤忘食、樂以忘憂、不知老之將至云爾. In Legge it ends with '?' because it sits inside 'Why did you not say...'. As a statement it is fine. '(of knowledge)' is Legge's own addition and may be cut. Leave out the Duke of She (a ruler). Not in the used list. 'Old age is coming on' is gentle, not morbid.

verified.quote: Eat to eight parts in ten, and you will need no doctor.
verified.original: 腹八分目に医者いらず
verified.who: Japanese proverb
verified.source: Kotowaza o Shiru Jiten, on Kotobank; variant 腹八合に医者いらず; usage example from Murai Gensai, Kuidoraku, 1903
verified.meaning: For good health, stop eating at about 80% full, not stuffed.
verified.reason: The Kotobank entry confirms the headword, the definition (健康のためには、満腹するまで食べないで、八分目ぐらいでやめておくのがよい), the variant 腹八合に医者いらず and the 1903 Kuidoraku example. The quote is fine. I changed the meaning line to follow the dictionary definition. The old line, 'you'll rarely need a doctor', reads like a medical promise or advice to skip doctors. Not in the used list. Add no Okinawa or longevity numbers.

verified.quote: Health is the head of everything, dearest of all.
verified.original: Здоровье — всему голова, всего дороже.
verified.who: Russian proverb
verified.source: V. I. Dal, Poslovitsy russkogo naroda (Proverbs of the Russian People), 1862, section 'Здоровье — хворь' (Health and Illness)
verified.meaning: Good health comes first; it is worth more than anything.
verified.reason: I fetched the Wikisource page and found 'Здоровье — всему голова, всего дороже.' in the section 'Здоровье — хворь'. 'Береги платье снову, а здоровье смолоду' is also on the same page, confirmed. The lines next to it are about strokes and wounds, so do not use them. The translation is faithful (всему голова means 'the main thing'). None of the Dal proverbs in the used list are this one.

verified.quote: If you live long, there is much joy and much benefit. Day by day you come to know what you did not know; month by month you become able to do what you could not do.
verified.original: 長生すれば、楽多く益多し。日々にいまだ知らざる事をしり、月々にいまだ能せざる事をよくす。
verified.who: Kaibara Ekiken, physician and scholar
verified.source: Yojokun (Lessons on Nourishing Life), book 1 (総論上), section 119 in the Nakamura Gakuen University Kaibara Ekiken Archive text, 1713; literal translation
verified.meaning: Live long, and every day you learn and can do something new.
verified.reason: The Nakamura Gakuen archive page now loads. It sits under 巻第一 総論上, section [119], and has exactly 長生すれば、楽多く益多し。日々にいまだ知らざる事をしり、月々にいまだ能せざる事をよくす, so the classical wording is confirmed. The KADOKAWA page for Matsumiya's modern translation (published 25 May 2026) gives the same passage in modern Japanese. The section opens with a line about dying before fifty, and that is correctly left out. Different from the two Yojokun passages already used. Confidence raised to high.

verified.quote: The people of high antiquity who knew the Way... were moderate in eating and drinking, regular in rising and resting, and did not wear themselves out recklessly. So body and spirit stayed together, and they lived out their full natural years.
verified.original: 上古之人，其知道者……食飲有節，起居有常，不妄作勞，故能形與神俱，而盡終其天年
verified.who: Qibo, the physician who answers in the Huangdi Neijing
verified.source: Huangdi Neijing Suwen (Basic Questions), ch. 1, 上古天真論 (On the True Nature of High Antiquity); literal translation
verified.meaning: People who ate moderately, kept regular habits and didn't overstrain lived full lives.
verified.reason: I fetched the Wikisource page and confirmed 岐伯對曰：上古之人，其知道者，法於陰陽，和於術數，食飲有節，起居有常，不妄作勞，故能形與神俱，而盡終其天年，度百歲乃去. The '...' leaves out 法於陰陽，和於術數, which is correct. The translation is faithful. Leave out the Yellow Emperor's question, the 'hundred years' line (it describes an ideal past, not a record) and the 今時之人 lines that follow (wine, excess). Suwen ch. 2 and 23 are used, and ch. 1 is new. Credit Qibo or 'Suwen', not the Emperor.

verified.quote: Remember then: there is only one time that is important—Now! It is the most important time because it is the only time when we have any power.
verified.original: Так и помни, что самое важное время одно: сейчас, а самое важное оно потому, что в нем одном мы властны над собой;
verified.who: Leo Tolstoy (a hermit's answer in his story)
verified.source: 'Three Questions' (Три вопроса), 1903; tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude, in Twenty-Three Tales (1906)
verified.meaning: The most important time is now, the only time we can act.
verified.reason: The English matches word for word in Chapter 23 of the online text of Twenty-Three Tales (1906), the Maude translation (both Maudes died in 1938-39, so it is public domain). I checked the Russian in the Yandex Books reader. It matches exactly, and the book's note gives first publication in Moscow, 1903. Maude's 'any power' is a fair rendering of 'властны над собой'. The long dash is Maude's own; on a slide, 'important: Now!' is fine. Use only the hermit's words, with no king, no wounded man and no backstory about the 1903 charity book. Not one of the Tolstoy texts already used.

verified.quote: I respectfully say to all who study the mystery: do not let your time pass in vain.
verified.original: 謹白參玄人，光陰莫虛度。
verified.who: Shitou Xiqian (700-790), Chan master
verified.source: Cantongqi (Japanese: Sandokai), closing lines; in the Zutangji (952), ch. 4 (光陰勿虛度), and the Jingde Chuandeng Lu, ch. 30 (Taisho T51, p. 459b20); chanted daily in Soto Zen; literal translation
verified.meaning: To all who practise: don't let your time slip away wasted.
verified.reason: The CBETA full-text API confirms 謹白參玄人。光陰莫虛(度) in the Jingde Chuandeng Lu ch. 30 (T51, 459b20). The Zutangji ch. 4 has 謹白參玄人，光陰勿虛(度). The sacred-texts mirror shows the same closing lines. I changed the translation because the item's 'do not let your days and nights pass in vain' was almost word for word the modern Soto liturgy English ('do not pass your days and nights in vain'), which is probably copyrighted. The new version is literal (光陰 = time). The meaning line was adjusted to match. Respectful to the tradition. Not in the used list.

verified.quote: Fast flies meanwhile the irreparable hour.
verified.original: Sed fugit interea, fugit inreparabile tempus. (Latin. Literal: 'But meanwhile it flies, time flies, never to be regained.')
verified.who: Virgil, Roman poet (70-19 BC)
verified.source: Georgics III.284, tr. James Rhoades, The Georgics of Virgil (2nd ed., Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner, London, 1891; also in Rhoades's Oxford edition, 1921)
verified.meaning: Time keeps flying away, and we can never get it back.
verified.credit: Virgil · Georgics III, tr. James Rhoades
verified.reason: The Gutenberg #232 text (translator James Rhoades) has exactly 'Fast flies meanwhile the irreparable hour,' at the end of the horse-breeding section of Book III. At The Latin Library the Latin is 'Sed fugit interea, fugit inreparabile tempus' at line 284 (285 follows it), so the line number is right. This is the source of 'tempus fugit'. A web search confirmed the 2nd edition (Kegan Paul, 1891) and a 1921 Oxford printing. The first-edition date is still unconfirmed, so cite the 2nd edition. The lines around it describe mares in season, hippomanes 'poisonous juice' and a youth swimming a storm-tossed sea, so quote only this one line. Note for translators: 'irreparable' means 'cannot be got back', not 'damaged'. Not in the used list.

verified.quote: We do not have a very short time assigned to us, but we lose a great deal of it: life is long enough to carry out the most important projects...
verified.original: Non exiguum temporis habemus, sed multum perdidimus. Satis longa vita et in maximarum rerum consummationem large data est, si tota bene collocaretur.
verified.who: Seneca, Roman Stoic philosopher (c. 4 BC-AD 65)
verified.source: On the Shortness of Life (De Brevitate Vitae) I.3, tr. Aubrey Stewart, in L. Annaeus Seneca, Minor Dialogues, Bohn's Classical Library, George Bell and Sons, London, 1889, p. 288
verified.meaning: Life is long enough if we use it well and stop wasting it.
verified.credit: Seneca · On the Shortness of Life
verified.reason: Matched word for word in the archive.org scan (title page: George Bell and Sons, London, 1889). The sentence goes on: '...have an ample portion, if we do but arrange the whole of it aright', which supports the meaning line. The Latin Library has the Latin at section 1.3, exactly as given. The ch. IX line 'postponement is the greatest waste of life... live now straightway' is also confirmed in the same scan. The researcher is right to warn about the popular line, which comes from a modern copyrighted translation. Not in the used list (the Seneca passages already used are Letters 2, 6, 44, 54, 55, 71, 104 and On Providence).

verified.quote: ...hold every hour in your grasp. Lay hold of to-day's task, and you will not need to depend so much upon to-morrow's. While we are postponing, life speeds by.
verified.original: omnes horas complectere; sic fiet ut minus ex crastino pendeas, si hodierno manum inieceris. Dum differtur vita transcurrit.
verified.who: Seneca, Roman Stoic philosopher
verified.source: Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 1 ('On Saving Time') 1.2-3, tr. Richard M. Gummere, Loeb Classical Library vol. I, 1917
verified.meaning: Use every hour. Do today's work today; while we delay, life rushes past.
verified.credit: Seneca · Letters to Lucilius 1, tr. Gummere
verified.reason: Matched word for word in Gummere's text on Wikisource. The Latin Library has 'omnes horas complectere... manum inieceris' in §2 and 'Dum differtur vita transcurrit' at the start of §3, so '1.2-3' is right. The opening '...' honestly cuts 'Therefore, Lucilius, do as you write me that you are doing:'. The lines just before it ('dying daily', 'death's hands') are rightly left out. Letter 1 is not in the used list.

verified.quote: He has half the deed done, who has made a beginning. Boldly undertake the study of true wisdom: begin it forthwith.
verified.original: Dimidium facti, qui coepit, habet; sapere aude, incipe.
verified.who: Horace, Roman poet (65-8 BC)
verified.source: Epistles I.2, lines 40-41, tr. C. Smart, revised by T. A. Buckley, The Works of Horace (Harper & Brothers, New York, 1863)
verified.meaning: Starting is half the job. Be brave and begin learning wisdom right now.
verified.credit: Horace · Epistles I.2, tr. C. Smart
verified.reason: Matched exactly in Gutenberg #14020 (Smart, revised by Buckley). The Latin Library has 'Dimidium facti, qui coepit, habet; sapere aude,' at line 40, followed by 'incipe.', so lines 40-41 is right. The Perseus catalog confirms the Harper & Brothers 1863 revised edition. The flagged context is real and is rightly cut. Just before: 'Robbers rise by night, that they may cut men's throats', and dropsy. Just after: the hind waiting for the river to run off (a water image). The Goethe/Anster misattribution flag is correct. Not in the used list.

verified.quote: Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might...
verified.original: כֹּל אֲשֶׁר תִּמְצָא יָדְךָ לַעֲשׂוֹת בְּכֹחֲךָ עֲשֵׂה (Hebrew, Ecclesiastes 9:10)
verified.who: Ecclesiastes (Hebrew Bible)
verified.source: Ecclesiastes 9:10, King James Version, 1611
verified.meaning: Whatever job you find to do, do it with all your strength.
verified.reason: BibleGateway's KJV reads: 'Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest.' The '...' honestly cuts the clause about the grave. Sefaria's Hebrew (Miqra according to the Masorah) matches the given Hebrew once the cantillation marks are removed. A different passage from the used Ecclesiastes 3:1. Credit the book, not the traditional royal author.

verified.quote: In the morning when thou risest unwillingly, let this thought be present,--I am rising to the work of a human being.
verified.original: Ὄρθρου, ὅταν δυσόκνως ἐξεγείρῃ, πρόχειρον ἔστω ὅτι ἐπὶ ἀνθρώπου ἔργον ἐγείρομαι
verified.who: Marcus Aurelius, Stoic philosopher (121-180)
verified.source: Meditations V.1, tr. George Long, 1862
verified.meaning: On sleepy mornings, remember you are getting up to do a person's real work.
verified.credit: Marcus Aurelius · Meditations V.1, tr. Long
verified.reason: Matched exactly at the start of Book V in Gutenberg #15877 (translator George Long). Perseus (Meditations 5.1) has the Greek exactly as given. The '--' is a long dash in print, so the designer can use a colon. The extra line in the same section, 'it is necessary to take rest also... Nature has fixed bounds to this too: she has fixed bounds to eating and drinking', is confirmed. Only IV.23 is in the used list. Present him as a Stoic writer, not as an emperor.

verified.quote: When I dance, I dance; when I sleep, I sleep.
verified.original: Quand je dance, je dance ; quand je dors, je dors
verified.who: Michel de Montaigne, French essayist (1533-1592)
verified.source: Essays III.13 'Of Experience', tr. Charles Cotton (1685-86), ed. W. Carew Hazlitt (1877)
verified.meaning: Whatever I am doing, I give it my whole attention.
verified.reason: Matched in Gutenberg #3600 (Cotton, ed. Hazlitt) in 'Of Experience'. The orchard sentence that follows is confirmed, and so is the 'so short in time... deeper and fuller' line. fr.wikisource (Essais III.13) has 'Quand je dance, je dance ; quand je dors, je dors'. FIX, meaning line only: the old line 'my whole mind dances' added an image Montaigne does not use. His point, as the orchard sentence shows, is giving full attention to what you are doing now. Context check: a few lines earlier there is a mild joke about scholars 'even when on their wives', so quote only this line or this line plus the orchard sentence. Only 'Of Pedantry' and the calf story have been used before.

verified.quote: Now there are short and simple exercises which tire the body rapidly, and so save our time; and time is something of which we ought to keep strict account. These exercises are running, brandishing weights, and jumping...
verified.original: Sunt exercitationes et faciles et breves, quae corpus et sine mora lassent et tempori parcant, cuius praecipua ratio habenda est: cursus et cum aliquo pondere manus motae et saltus...
verified.who: Seneca, Roman Stoic philosopher
verified.source: Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 15 ('On Brawn and Brains') 15.4, tr. Richard M. Gummere, Loeb Classical Library vol. I, 1917
verified.meaning: Quick, simple exercise like running and jumping works the body fast and saves time.
verified.credit: Seneca · Letters to Lucilius 15, tr. Gummere
verified.reason: Matched word for word in §4 on Wikisource (Gummere). The Latin Library confirms the Latin starts in §4. The '...' honestly cuts 'high-jumping or broad-jumping, or... the Priest's dance'. §5 is confirmed: 'come back soon from body to mind... need not be hampered by... old age. Cultivate that good which improves with the years.' The context is fairly described: §2-3 warn against heavy bodybuilding and overeating, and §3 mentions slaves, so leave it out. Letter 15 is not in the used list (Letter 55 is a different letter).

verified.quote: ...to adopt a regimen of health; to practise moderate exercise; and to take just enough of food and drink to restore our strength and not to overburden it.
verified.original: habenda ratio valetudinis, utendum exercitationibus modicis, tantum cibi et potionis adhibendum ut reficiantur vires, non opprimantur.
verified.who: Cicero, Roman philosopher and writer (106-43 BC), in his dialogue On Old Age
verified.source: Cato Maior de Senectute (On Old Age) 35-36, tr. W. A. Falconer, Loeb Classical Library, 1923
verified.meaning: Have healthy habits, exercise gently, and eat and drink just enough, not too much.
verified.credit: Cicero · On Old Age, tr. Falconer
verified.reason: Matched on LacusCurtius (Loeb 1923, public domain). The §36 marker falls between 'regimen of health;' and 'to practise', so '35-36' is right. The Latin Library has the Latin exactly as given. The cut clause ('to fight against it as we would fight against disease') is rightly left out. Also confirmed: §34 'by exercise and self-control, even in old age, to preserve some of his original vigour' (the example just before it is King Masinissa, so do not name him) and §32 'I am in my eighty-fourth year' (Cato, a character in the dialogue, not an age record). Keep the speaker's military and political career out. Cicero is not in the used list.

verified.quote: Though I look old, yet I am strong and lusty; / For in my youth I never did apply / Hot and rebellious liquors in my blood... / Therefore my age is as a lusty winter, / Frosty, but kindly.
verified.original: Same (English, c. 1599).
verified.who: William Shakespeare (the old servant Adam, 'almost fourscore', i.e. nearly 80)
verified.source: As You Like It, Act 2, Scene 3 (c. 1599)
verified.meaning: I am old but strong, because I did not harm my body when young.
verified.credit: Shakespeare · As You Like It, Act 2 Sc. 3
verified.reason: Matched on the MIT Shakespeare site, including the cut lines 'Nor did not with unbashful forehead woo / The means of weakness and debility'. 'almost fourscore' is confirmed later in the same scene. Adam is fictional, so his age is not a record. CAUTION, as flagged: 'lusty' means vigorous here. The cut lines most likely hint at youthful wildness, and today's readers may take 'lusty' as sexual, so translators must render it as 'vigorous' or 'full of strength'. The scene's plot (a brother's plan to burn Orlando's lodging) must not be mentioned. Only Romeo and Juliet has been used before.

verified.quote: ...life is not living, but living in health.
verified.original: Non est vivere, sed valere vita est.
verified.who: Martial, Roman poet (c. AD 40-104)
verified.source: Epigrams VI.70, line 15, tr. Walter C. A. Ker, Loeb Classical Library, Martial: Epigrams vol. I, 1919
verified.meaning: Real life is not just staying alive; it is living in good health.
verified.reason: The archive.org scan of Ker's Loeb vol. I (title page Heinemann/Putnam, MCMXIX, preface dated April 22, 1919) has, in VI.70: '...is much deceived and mistaken : life is not living, but living in health.' The facing Latin line 15 reads 'non est vivere, sed valere vita est.', matching the Latin Library. Strictly, the poem is addressed to Marcianus and is about Cotta, who is past 62. Confirmed that the middle has the 'insulting finger' and lists fevers and pains, so quote only the last line, as advised. Martial is not in the used list.

rejected.who: Leo Tolstoy (the hermit's answer in his story)
rejected.reason: The wording itself is confirmed: Gutenberg #6157 (Maude translation) has the exact text. I reject it on content safety. The hermit is speaking to a KING, and the whole plot is a man whose brother the king executed coming to kill him. That puts monarchy, an execution and an assassination plot right behind the quote, which is risky for a Thai audience even if the slide never mentions the king, because anyone who looks up the source gets that story. Tolstoy also wrote the story in 1903 for Sholem Aleichem's anthology to help pogrom victims (Wikipedia, 'Esarhaddon, King of Assyria'; Popoff), which touches religious violence. I could not open the Russian original to check the translation. When unsure, reject. W3 and W4 already cover dont_wait safely.

rejected.who: Antonio Stradivari, violin maker, Cremona (c. 1644 to 1737)
rejected.reason: The age claim is disputed. Tarisio's own 'Belle Skinner' entry (ID 40113) says 'current historians believe' most of the 'D'Anni 9x' inscriptions were written by Count Cozio, who 'wished to memorialize his theory of the maker's age'. It says the 1644 birth year 'is not supported by archival documents'. Wikipedia's Muntz article also says Cozio may have written it. So 'still making violins in his nineties' rests on a label he may not have written, and the reasoning goes in a circle. When unsure, reject. It is also not really a quote.
